forward.prompt:
These are the eligible OVERVIEW photographs of one clothing SKU. Detail/closeup photographs have been excluded. Each VIEW contains its original photograph and SAM3 mask regions.
R001, R002, etc. are UNIQUE addresses of pixels, NOT garment identities. Different views ALWAYS have different region IDs. Match the clothing visually across those DIFFERENT IDs. Never require an ID to repeat across views.
Find each visually distinct garment with at least one usable region in EVERY shown VIEW. One garment may occupy MULTIPLE SAM3 masks in one view and ONE mask in another. A dress's bodice, waist panel, sleeves and attached skirt are parts of the SAME dress, not separate garments merely because SAM3 split them. A seam, change of transparency, pose or front/back appearance does not establish a different garment. Use the full photographs to identify construction and physical garment extent. In contrast, a separately visible shirt under a vest/jacket remains a distinct visual layer, even if sewn together. Matching color alone is insufficient. Mixed masks are not usable.
Only a visible portion is required in an overview; do not require full silhouettes. Keep repeated styling too when present in every shown view. Do not select by the item for sale. Do not invent new mask boundaries.
Return JSON only: {"reason":"brief visual comparison", "tracks":[{"garment":"description", "regions":["R001", "R004"]}]}. The IDs here are schema examples, not an answer. Each track must list actual supplied IDs covering EVERY shown VIEW, including all confirmed parts of that garment. Assign a region to at most one track. Unlisted regions are removed. If no garment is visibly supported everywhere, return an empty tracks list.
forward.raw: {"reason": "The white button-up shirt appears in all three views, consistently showing the same collar, placket, and fabric texture. In v0, it is shown front (R001) and back (R002). In v1, the front is shown again (R003) and the back is partially visible (R004). In v2, the front is shown again (R005). The back view in v1 (R004) is a partial view but matches the same garment as R002. The white skirt (R006) appears only in v2 and is not present in v0 or v1, so it cannot be tracked across all views. Therefore, only the white shirt is consistently visible across all views.", "tracks": [{"garment": "white button-up shirt", "regions": ["R001", "R002", "R003", "R004", "R005"]}]}

all_view_rule: Every eligible overview must support a visible part of the same garment. Closeups are excluded from both matching and context. No full silhouette is required.

identity.prompt:
Classify this retail photograph by its photographic composition, NOT by the clothing category or whether the full person is visible.
OVERVIEW: a normal front/back/side outfit or garment view, or a product-only photograph showing the overall object. A headless model, cropped legs, partial occlusion, or a small accessory filling the image does not by itself make a detail shot. A complete product photograph is an overview.
CLOSEUP: a deliberate tight detail shot of only a garment subsection, such as fabric, neckline, shoulder/back opening, fastener, label, waist or hem. The overall garment extent is outside the frame. These detail photographs are excluded from a later matching task.
UNCERTAIN: you cannot distinguish these photographic roles. Never guess based on file names or an item's title.
Return only JSON: {"role":"overview|closeup|uncertain", "reason":"brief explanation of the visible framing"}. Choose exactly one role.

Although the front view is cropped at the waist, the overall garment structure is clearly presented, consistent with a standard product overview composition."}

identity.prompt:
Image 1 is the unaltered full SOURCE photograph. Image 2 shows that same photograph with REGION 1 outlined blue and REGION 2 red. Images 3 and 4 isolate the two regions' exact pixels. All regions come from the SAME photograph. Are these pixels fragments of ONE visually distinct garment? First locate the marked pixels in the unaltered photograph and identify the fabric underneath them. SAM3 can split a plain fabric body into a main mask and many disconnected interior islands: an irregular or speckled mask shape does not mean background. A collar, sleeve, hem, printed graphic, or interior fabric island can belong to the main garment. Use the source positions and visible garment boundaries, not only crop colors or mask shapes. A dress's bodice and attached skirt are parts of ONE dress, including when separated by a waist seam or mesh panel. Use the source construction to distinguish these from two independent clothes. Separate upper and lower garments and neighboring layers remain DIFFERENT even when the fabric matches or the layers are sewn into one product. Do not join different clothes merely because they touch or share a color. Actual background pixels, mixed unrelated masks, and genuinely unidentifiable contents must not be joined.
A: same visually distinct garment
B: different garments, object or background
C: uncertain or mixed

contextual_review.prompt:
All four images refer to ONE source photograph. Image 1 is the unaltered source. Image 2 marks region 1 blue and region 2 red. Images 3 and 4 isolate their exact pixels. Identify the fabric or background actually underneath each marked region. Mask shape is not garment identity: one SAM3 region can be many disconnected fabric islands. A shirt's sleeve, body, hem, neck, and printed graphic are parts of the SAME garment. A dress's bodice, mesh waist panel, sleeves and attached skirt are parts of ONE dress, not separate clothes merely because SAM3 split them. Two distinct pieces of clothing, such as a vest above a skirt or a jacket over a shirt, remain DIFFERENT even if their fabric matches or they are manufactured together. Compare source positions and actual fabric contents. A mask mixing unrelated garments is uncertain.
Return JSON only with four fields in this order. Keep each description under 15 words and the reason under 40 words. Do not repeat the instructions or debate the meaning of garment parts.
{"region1":"source contents", "region2":"source contents", "reason":"explanation using source positions and garment boundaries", "verdict":"A"}
Use verdict A for the same visually distinct garment, B for different garments/objects/background, or C for uncertain/mixed. The A in the schema is an example, not the answer.

No separate garments or background are visible.", "verdict":"A"}
